title: Modified FOLFOX-6

agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

phases_note: The treating team confirms the indication, schedule and duration. Changes are recorded on your own prescription.
medicines_title: Your medicines and what they do
timeline_note: Bars show planned treatment and possible symptom patterns, not measured risk. Side effects can overlap and persist.
safety_note: There are no guaranteed safe days. Act on fever, sudden illness or a new serious symptom whenever it occurs. Do not wait for the next appointment.
teachback: Can you explain which medicines you are receiving, the schedule, the contact plan and the symptoms that need prompt help?
consent_support: Confirm DPD testing, pump and line care, disconnection arrangements, cold precautions and anti-sickness instructions.
urgent_extra: New chest pain, breathing difficulty, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, reduced urine, uncontrolled bleeding or a rapidly worsening symptom needs prompt assessment.

chapters.title: Your indication and treatment aim
chapters.intro: The same medicines can have different aims.

items.title: After colon-cancer surgery
items.text: Adjuvant treatment aims to reduce recurrence risk after complete resection. The likely absolute benefit depends on stage, pathology, fitness and other features. Ask how recurrence risk and neuropathy risk influence the proposed duration.

items.title: Advanced colorectal or upper-GI cancer
items.text: Treatment may aim to control growth, relieve symptoms and prolong life. The plan is reviewed against response, toxicity and your priorities. A treatment break or a change of components requires an individual discussion.

items.title: How long will treatment last?
items.text: Do not infer duration from the number of passport pages. Ask for the planned number of cycles and review points. The NCCP schedule distinguishes adjuvant colon treatment, metastatic colorectal treatment and upper-GI treatment.

chapters.title: Living with the 46-hour pump
chapters.intro: Ask for a demonstration and written contact instructions.

items.title: Before leaving
items.text: Know what normal pump progress looks like, how to carry it and how to protect the line while washing or sleeping. Check who will disconnect it and when. Have the team check anything you do not understand.

items.title: Leakage or a delivery problem
items.text: Use the hospital spill instructions, avoid direct contact with leaked medicine and call the team. Do not repair a connection or adjust the pump. A pump finishing much sooner or later than expected also needs advice.

items.title: Chest pain while on fluorouracil
items.text: Fluorouracil can affect the heart. New chest pain during treatment needs urgent assessment; severe pain, collapse or major breathing difficulty means 112/999. Tell emergency staff that fluorouracil is infusing. Follow the team’s instructions about the pump.

chapters.title: What the checks are for
chapters.intro: Symptoms, blood results and the treatment aim answer different questions.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils protect against infection, haemoglobin carries oxygen and platelets help clotting. A normal previous result or feeling well does not prove the current counts are safe. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate advice.

items.title: Kidney and liver function
items.text: Organ function can change drug exposure. Vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and worsen kidney function. Report reduced urine, poor intake, jaundice and new medicines. The clinical assessment combines results with symptoms.

items.title: Describe symptoms in practical terms
items.text: Tell the team about the worst symptoms since the last visit, even if improved today. Examples include extra stools above your usual pattern, whether mouth pain affects drinking, and whether numbness affects buttons or balance.

items.title: How benefit is assessed
items.text: After surgery, treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence; there may be no visible cancer to measure. In advanced disease, scans, symptoms and function help assess control. Ask when review is planned and what would lead to a change.

chapters.title: Recognising treatment effects
chapters.intro: Early reporting helps the team manage symptoms and protect function.

items.title: Acute cold sensitivity and persistent neuropathy
items.text: Cold-related tingling can occur soon after oxaliplatin. Persistent numbness between cycles is different and may worsen with repeated treatment. Describe duration and effect on hand use or walking. Some neuropathy can remain after treatment ends.

items.title: Bowel and mouth symptoms
items.text: Fluorouracil can affect rapidly renewing tissues. Keep track of stools compared with your normal pattern, including stoma output. Report diarrhoea, painful ulcers or reduced drinking; do not wait for the next cycle if you are dehydrated or unwell.

items.title: Hand-foot soreness and skin changes
items.text: Tell the team about red, tender or peeling palms or soles. Reduce friction and use the skin care recommended locally. Pain limiting normal activity needs review. Do not assume it must be tolerated to complete treatment.

items.title: Fatigue and nausea
items.text: Use manageable activity, rest and the prescribed anti-sickness plan. New profound weakness, faintness or breathlessness warrants assessment because anaemia, infection, dehydration and other problems can look like ordinary fatigue.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Plan around the activities and people that matter to you.

items.title: Food, drink and practical help
items.text: Use foods and drinks you can manage. Tell the team about weight loss, poor intake or difficulty shopping and cooking; ask for dietitian or practical support. A fixed daily fluid target is not appropriate for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney problems.

items.title: Activity, rest and driving
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Record what fatigue stops you doing. Do not drive when dizzy, unwell or affected by sedating medicines. Ask about work adjustments and transport for treatment days.

items.title: Medicines, vaccines and supplements
items.text: Bring a complete medicine list, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Ask the oncology pharmacist before changes. Discuss vaccination timing. Do not stop prescribed long-term medicines on your own.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment when relevant. Ask for a written contraception and breastfeeding plan covering each medicine and the period after treatment. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy.

items.title: Support for you and your family
items.text: Ask about psycho-oncology, social work, counselling and symptom support. Take information in manageable amounts. A family member or trusted person can help record questions if you wish. Discuss how treatment fits your priorities.

chapters.title: Words you may hear
chapters.intro: A short reference for clinic discussions.

items.title: Adjuvant, metastatic and cycle
items.text: Adjuvant means treatment after the main treatment, usually surgery, to reduce recurrence risk. Metastatic means spread to a distant site. A cycle includes treatment and the interval before the next planned start.

items.title: DPD, neuropathy and dose modification
items.text: DPD is an enzyme involved in fluorouracil breakdown. Neuropathy means nerve damage or dysfunction. Dose modification means changing the amount, timing or components to balance benefit and harm.

purpose: Modified FOLFOX-6 combines oxaliplatin, folinic acid and fluorouracil. It can be used after colon-cancer surgery or to treat advanced colorectal, stomach or gastro-oesophageal-junction cancer. The aim and duration depend on the indication; ask which applies to you.
schedule_summary: Day 1: oxaliplatin, folinic acid and fluorouracil, followed by a 46-hour fluorouracil pump. A cycle lasts 14 days.

phases.label: 14-day treatment cycle
phases.detail: Day 1: oxaliplatin, folinic acid and fluorouracil, followed by a 46-hour fluorouracil pump. A cycle lasts 14 days.

timeline.label: Blood counts / infection
timeline.text: Timing varies; no guaranteed safe days

day_groups.title: Infusion and pump connection
day_groups.body: Symptoms and blood tests are reviewed. The day-ward medicines are followed by connection of a fluorouracil pump. Tell the nurse immediately about a reaction or pain at the infusion site.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm the pump-care instructions, disconnection appointment and contact number.

day_groups.title: The pump is delivering treatment
day_groups.body: The infusion runs for about 46 hours from connection; the calendar day does not determine the exact finish time. Follow the instructions for keeping the line dry and secure. Avoid cold exposure if it triggers symptoms.
day_groups.action: Call for a leaking, disconnected or unexpectedly stopped pump. Do not reconnect, alter settings or disconnect it yourself unless specifically trained and instructed.

day_groups.title: After disconnection
day_groups.body: Nausea, diarrhoea, mouth symptoms, fatigue or cold sensitivity may continue. Use prescribed support. New symptoms deserve advice even if the pump has finished.
day_groups.action: Report poor intake, persistent diarrhoea or mouth pain early. Chest pain or major breathing difficulty requires emergency help.

day_groups.title: Between visits and the next review
day_groups.body: Blood counts can fall between visits. Numbness may accumulate over cycles. Describe any difficulty fastening buttons, walking or handling objects before more oxaliplatin.
day_groups.action: Bring the symptom passport and check the next appointment. Day 1 usually repeats 14 days after this cycle started, only if confirmed.

support.title: DPD testing before fluorouracil
support.text: DPD helps the body break down fluorouracil. Deficiency can cause severe toxicity. Testing guides the plan but cannot exclude all serious reactions; unexpectedly severe early diarrhoea, mouth sores or illness needs immediate review.

support.title: Cold precautions
support.text: Oxaliplatin can trigger cold-related nerve symptoms. Avoid cold drinks and direct cold exposure if advised. Do not use ice chips during this regimen. Throat tightness or breathing difficulty needs assessment; do not assume it is harmless cold sensitivity.

support.title: Pump and line care
support.text: Check the pump and line as taught. Keep the disconnection appointment and written spill instructions. Pain, swelling, redness, leakage, a wet dressing or a change in pump delivery needs contact with the team.

support.title: Anti-sickness support
support.text: Take prescribed preventive medicines and keep the breakthrough plan available. Some anti-sickness medicines cause constipation. Ask for review if symptoms are poorly controlled.

evidence.title: Evidence depends on your cancer setting
evidence.intro: The numbers below concern resected stage III colon cancer, not every indication on this page.
evidence.population: MOSAIC studied 2,246 patients with resected stage II or III colon cancer. It compared FOLFOX4 with fluorouracil/folinic acid. The illustrated subgroup is stage III.

metrics.label: Stage III: alive at ten years

evidence.interpretation: The difference was 8.1 percentage points. This is regimen-family evidence: FOLFOX4 is not identical to modified FOLFOX-6. These figures do not estimate benefit for stage II, metastatic colorectal or upper-GI cancer, or predict an individual outcome.

chronology_notes.title: Treatment and pump
chronology_notes.text: Day 1 treatment is followed by a 46-hour fluorouracil infusion. The team confirms the exact pump disconnection time.

chronology_notes.title: Cold sensitivity
chronology_notes.text: Tingling or throat discomfort can occur early and may persist; follow the precautions your team gives you.

chronology_notes.title: Blood counts
chronology_notes.text: Counts can fall between visits. The day of the cycle and how well you feel cannot rule out infection.

chronology_notes.title: Symptoms over time
chronology_notes.text: Mouth and bowel symptoms or fatigue can overlap. Numbness may accumulate across cycles; describe changes before the next dose.
